items.question: Why is an omitted dependency acceptable in a model boundary only when it cannot change the comparison under the declared conditions?
core_claims: A model boundary separates the model's own state from the rest of the world and is not the same as a service boundary or a team boundary.
An omitted actor, dependency or failure is acceptable only if the omitted part cannot change the comparison under the declared conditions.
Replacing a downstream timeout with a constant service time removes the failure that motivates the decision, so the model can no longer show the effect being compared.
A boundary placed after request admission can reverse a result when the decision concerns a caller-visible outcome.
A reviewable scope statement records purpose, alternatives, deciding observable, excluded items and validity range so a reader can challenge whether each exclusion is material.
optional_claims: A stock-and-flow model can show utilization and backlog growth at 20 requests per second against 24 per second but cannot report the p95 latency of successful requests.
Sargent separates conceptual-model validity from operational validity, and a scope statement addresses only the conceptual side.

items.question: Why can a model contract pass every automated check and still misstate its evidence?
core_claims: The validator checks strict schema conformance, a unique tycho.model identifier, scenario resolution to that identifier, and the presence of a source and measurement record for every parameter marked measured.
It cannot check that a cited source actually supports the parameter value, so linking the label to the record remains an editorial and review task.
The schema rejects a verification case that lacks a test path or an observed result, but it cannot detect a case that claims a pass without one.
Unit fields make a state-versus-rate mismatch visible, yet the validator performs no dimensional analysis.
An orphan model, a scenario override that leaves the calibration note stale, and an assumed value copied into a measured field all survive structural validation.
optional_claims: An uncalibrated status is a complete contract value rather than a missing field.
The contract makes a model's claims inspectable; it does not prove that the model is useful.

items.question: Why can a larger bounded queue lower the rejection rate while increasing the share of requests lost to timeouts?
core_claims: Queue capacity bounds waiting requests and rejects arrivals once full, while the bulkhead and timeout impose separate admission limits.
A queue large enough to absorb arrivals rejects almost nothing: the overload run reports a rejection rate of 0.0005 with a mean queue length of 12.79 requests.
Waiting longer pushes requests past the one-second deadline, so 0.3495 of requests time out even though almost none are rejected.
The dominant loss mechanism therefore shifts from rejection to deadline expiry, and a report that focuses on rejection misses most of the loss.
Retries add attempts to an already saturated pool, so retry amplification raises load instead of creating capacity.
optional_claims: An unbounded queue never rejects, accumulates backlog and reports a latency that is an artifact of the observation horizon.
Exponential backoff with full jitter reduces synchronized retry waves, and the scenario must declare the choice for the run to be reproducible.

items.question: When does a simulated output require batch means instead of the independent-replication standard error?
core_claims: With n independent replications the standard error of the mean is s divided by the square root of n, and V12 gives each replication its own seed so replications are independent by construction.
Within a single replication, events are dependent by design, so a metric computed from one long run cannot use the independent-replication formula.
Batch means estimate the standard error by splitting one long run into batches, and V12 does not apply them because it uses independent replications.
The run's limitations must state which error method was used, and a future model based on one long run would need a different method.
V12 does not adapt the replication count during a run; the scenario declares it, and an adaptive rule would need its own seeded decision log.
optional_claims: A shared random stream across replications makes the reported standard error too small.
The stopping rule uses a pilot of at least ten replications to estimate the standard error, then computes the required n for the target relative error.

items.question: Why does a 100% target traffic share not establish that a cutover succeeded?
core_claims: Traffic share is one modeled stock, while dual-write backlog, accumulated divergence and the rollback drain are separate state variables with different failure modes.
A cutover state can expose a reconciliation backlog that legacy ownership had hidden, so serving traffic is not evidence that records reconcile.
In the staged run the target serves the synthetic load with success 1.0, yet maximum divergence reaches 8,925.5 records and rollback completes in only 10% of replications.
The false-cutover failure mode is treating a 100% traffic share as success while divergence is still growing.

A supported cutover requires measured lag and reconciliation capacity, a rehearsed rollback inside the observation window, sustained measured divergence below the business threshold and a confirmed runbook.
optional_claims: A shadow state can look healthy while the target's write path is untested, because the target receives traffic without owning the authoritative response.
Divergence is a synthetic proxy that accumulates when the dual-write backlog exceeds the reconciliation capacity, not a measured data-quality metric.

items.question: How can a V12 decision be decision-supported when every model input remains assumed?
core_claims: Decision evidence is a separate layer from calibration: it asks whether the outcome follows from the model and the declared constraints, not whether the inputs match a real system.
A decision-supported outcome with an uncalibrated model is conditional; it holds under the declared assumptions and does not claim that those assumptions are true.
The record must state the condition and the measurements that would reverse the decision.
Treating a recommendation as a deployment certificate crosses a layer boundary, because simulation success does not imply production success.
The checkout record can be decision-supported under its declared constraints while the operability constraint remains unverified, which makes the recommendation conditional.
optional_claims: The decision record can still rank what to measure first; it cannot substitute for the measurement.
